title: CHAPTER TWO. On the immortality of the soul, from the light of nature and the confession of barbarians, both ancient and recently discovered
english: CHAPTER TWO. On the immortality of the soul, from the light of nature and the confession of barbarians, both the ancient and those discovered in our own memory.

That our rational soul, free from destruction, survives after its departure from the body is shown by the light of nature and of Scripture, as by two torches shining in the dark. See our Alsted's Encyclopaedia, book 6, pneumatic part 4, chapter 2.

title: II. By the light of nature: Gentiles both barbarians and philosophers acknowledge immortality and care about the soul's state after this life
english: II. By the light of nature: because it has been received by common opinion that the Gentiles — both barbarians and philosophers — have acknowledged this, and on that account have been anxious about its state after this life.

title: III-IV. Barbarians ancient and recent; the ancient Getae and Egyptians (Herodotus, Diodorus)
english: III. Barbarians — both the ancient and those recently and newly discovered — have acknowledged it.

IV. The ancient, such as the Getae and the Egyptians. The Getae do not think that they themselves cease, but that he who has died goes across to Zamolxis. The Egyptians judge that their parents and ancestors have been translated to an eternal dwelling. Concerning the former Herodotus bears witness in book 4; concerning the latter Diodorus Siculus in book 1 of the Library, number 93.

title: V. Recently discovered peoples listed; whether the West Indies were known to the ancients; Fathers denied antipodes
english: V. The recent and newly discovered, such as the Guineans, Chinese, Peruvians, Mexicans, Guianans, Tupinamba, Brazilians, and Virginians.

I call these newly discovered. Yet it is not a curious question whether those regions which we now mark with the title of the West Indies were known to the ancient Greeks, Romans, and other nations. The holy Fathers once denied antipodes — Lactantius, Divine Institutes book 3, chapter 24; Augustine, City of God book 16, chapter 9. Indeed the constant opinion of those who asserted antipodes was that their region was wholly unknown to us — in Cicero, On the Republic book 6, and Pomponius Mela book 1, chapter 1 — and that it had still lain hidden in the secret of the divine mind, as Salmuth thought in his notes on Panciroli's New Discoveries, chapter 1; Jacob Martin, professor of Wittenberg, Miscellaneous Disputations, folio 599; Joseph Acosta, book 1, chapter 1.

title: Yet the New World may long have been partly known; Besoldus; Japheth origin; Fuller and others
english: Yet it is more likely that the islands, and the adjacent continent of that New World, were also long ago, many ages before, not wholly unknown to our world, as the polyhistor Christopher Besoldus, professor of Tubingen, demonstrates at length in his Political Discourses on the growth of empire, chapter 4, year 10; and the inhabitants are believed to have been of Cymbric or ancient Teutonic and Scythian origin from Japheth the son of Noah (Genesis 9:19, 27). Compare Nicholas Fuller, Theological Miscellanies book 1, chapter 4; Vandermylius On the Belgian Language chapter 25; Acosta book 1, chapter 24; Claude Duret, History of Languages chapter 78; Peter Bertius in his contracted maps of America; Johannes Goropius Becanus in the Antwerp Origins, in the Niloscopium; Lipsius, Stoic Physiology book 2, dissertation 19.

title: VI. The Guineans on another life and the last judgment; burial goods and royal funerary sacrifice
english: VI. THE GUINEANS, when asked about another life and the last judgment, answered that they indeed were wholly ignorant of the last day of judgment, yet affirmed that the account of men is one thing and that of cattle another; and although they were completely unaware of what becomes of people after deatht know whether that place to which they would be transferred was above or below the earth, they nonetheless usually assign some part of their household goods to the dead, so that wherever they finally arrive they may have what is necessary for daily uses.

So narrates the Description of the African kingdom of Guinea, chapter 21. And from this it is clear, says the author, that they somehow believe another life after this one survives, yet are wholly ignorant of the resurrection of the dead, estimating that as soon as they die they are transferred into another world, where they need varied household goods just as in this world: whence if they happen to lose something, they at once form thoughts of this sort — that perhaps some friend of theirs has come from the other world and carried it off because he could no longer do without it. The same author reports in chapter 44 that nobles, when a king has died, bestow some slave, and even slaughter a dearest wife and sons, so that they may be buried with the king and serve him in the other world.

title: VII. The Chinese: pagan religion; immortality and retribution; magnificent tombs (Linschoten)
english: VII. THE CHINESE, whose religion — without the contagion of Mohammedanism — is merely pagan, all believe the immortality of the soul, and after this life a retribution of goods or evils according as each has done good or evil things, and on that account they set up for the dead sepulchral monuments magnificently carved. They believe there is an immortal life in the other world, as Hugo Linschoten witnesses, part 1, chapter 25.

title: VIII. The Peruvians: immortality, eternal life and damnation (Acosta); ignorance of bodily resurrection; funerary slaves (Benzoni)
english: VIII. THE PERUVIANS believe the immortality of the soul and eternal life and death. Joseph Acosta, book 5, chapter 7: The Indians who dwell in Peru, he says, hold that the souls of men are immortal, and that eternal life awaits the pious, but eternal damnation the impious. And therefore they can easily be led to take up the faith of this article. But that bodies would one day rise again together with the souls themselves they were wholly ignorant. And from this he writes that it came about that, anxious about the other life, they slaughtered slaves at the funerals of their own, to minister there. Compare Girolamo Benzoni, History of the New World book 3, chapter 20.

title: IX-X. Mexicans profess the same faith; Guianans agree with Peruvians (Raleigh); burial with wives and treasures
english: IX. THE MEXICANS profess the same faith. For Acosta in chapter 8 reports nearly the same things, and that at the funerals of great men those who had been ready in serving the living were compelled by them to die, so that they might render the same services in the other age as well.

X. THE GUIANANS, Epicurean natives of the gold-bearing province, agree with the Peruvians in religion and opinions. For, as Walter Raleigh witnesses in his Description of Guiana, they believe the immortality of souls, adore the sun, and take care that the dearest wives they have had, as also their treasures, be buried with them: but the Orenoqueponi are not indeed buried with their wives, yet with all their treasures; they hope and believe that after these times they will again possess them.

title: XI. The Tupinamba of Brazil: fierce cannibals who believe soul-immortality; Lery on virtue, paradise, and Aygnan
english: XI. THE TUPINAMBA, Brazilians, believe the immortality of souls, being fierce and cannibals. For concerning them Jean de Lery, who spent a year among them, that he does not believe there is any nation in the whole globe of lands more alien from all religion: if nevertheless, by his own witness, they not only believed the immortality of souls, but also held it for certain that after death the souls of those who had cultivated virtue (but they define virtue in their own way — namely to take vengeance on enemies and to devour as many as possible), flying past the highest mountains, are gathered to the souls of their fathers and grandfathers, and there in most pleasant gardens spend a joyful age in perpetual delights and dances: but on the contrary the shades of the cowardly, who have lived without any care of defending the fatherland and ingloriously, are snatched away to Aygnan (so they call the evil demon) and live with him amid everlasting torments.

title: XII. The Virginians also believe soul-immortality; transfer to gods' seats or Popogusso (Hariot)
english: XII. THE VIRGINIANS also believe the immortality of the soul. For as soon as it is loosed from the body they hold that it is transferred according to the works it has done, either to the seats of the gods to enjoy perpetual happiness, or to a huge ditch or pit (which they judge to be situated at the furthest bounds of the world, far from themselves toward the west) unto perpetual fire. This place they themselves call Popogusso, as Thomas Hariot the Englishman related in his narrative of the commodities and rites of Virginia.

title: XIII. What barbarian confession shows: universal natural consensus; true light overlaid with false, vain, and impious additions — Cap. 2 close
english: XIII. This confession of the barbarians shows: 1. That concerning the immortality of the soul and its beatitude or misery after death there is a constant opinion among all nations, drawn from the principles of nature (as discussed in pneumatology), which may seem not so much learned as connate. For in every matter the consensus of all nations is to be counted the law of nature, as Cicero authorizes in Tusculan Disputations book 1; of which common consensus the vulgar opinions of the Gentiles, or the fables of shades, the Elysian fields, and Tartarus sung by the poets — Homer in Odyssey book 11, Virgil in Aeneid 6, and Ovid in Fasti book 2 — also give faith, which rest upon the immortality of the soul as a foundation from which they were born and without which they could not have been born.

2. That upon those things which are indeed true and legitimately deduced from the light of nature, the darknesses of the nations have built false, vain, and impious additions. It is true that souls are immortal, and that after their departure from the body it will go well or ill with them. It is false that happiness comes on account of victory won over external enemies. It is vain that household goods should be buried as if they would be of use in another world. And it is also impious and more than superstitious to slaughter human beings to that end, that provision may be made for the comforts of the dead in eternal life.
